## Problem 1

## Problem 2
```{r}
covar_df = 
  read_csv("data/nhanes_covar.csv", skip = 4) |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  filter(age >= 21) |> 
  drop_na() |> 
  mutate(
    sex = factor(sex, levels = c(1, 2), labels = c("male", "female")),
    education = factor(
      education, 
      levels = c(1, 2, 3), 
      labels = c("less than high school", "high school equivalent", "more than high school"),
      ordered = TRUE
    )
  )

accel_df = 
  read_csv("data/nhanes_accel.csv") |> 
  janitor::clean_names()

nhanes_df = inner_join(covar_df, accel_df, by = "seqn")

dim(nhanes_df)
```
Using NHANES demographic and accelerometer data, I kept participants that were 21+ with no missing demographic data, and then converted sex and education to labeled factors. I then merged them by ID. The resulting dataset contains 228 participants and 1445 variables (five demographic variables and 1440 activity measures).

```{r}
nhanes_df |> 
  count(education, sex) |> 
  pivot_wider(names_from = sex, values_from = n) |> 
  knitr::kable(
    caption = "Number of men and women in each education category",
    col.names = c("Education", "Male", "Female")
  )
```
More than high school contained the most participants. Male and Female are similar in the less than high school and more than high school groups. There are more men in the high school equivalent group.
```{r}
nhanes_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = sex, y = age, fill = sex)) + 
  geom_boxplot() + 
  facet_grid(. ~ education) + 
  labs(
    title = "Age distribution by sex and education level",
    x = "Sex",
    y = "Age (years)",
    fill = "Sex"
  )
```
High school equivalent females are older than the males. In more than high school, both males and females are younger. In less than high school, the age distribution for males and females look similar.

```{r}
total_df = 
  nhanes_df |> 
  mutate(total_activity = rowSums(pick(starts_with("min")))) |> 
  select(seqn, sex, age, education, total_activity)

total_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex)) + 
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) + 
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) + 
  facet_grid(. ~ education) + 
  labs(
    title = "Total daily activity by age, sex and education level",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Total daily activity (MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
  )
```
Across age groups, total activity declines with age. The trend line for men and women in the less than high school group are similar. In High school equivalent women are more active than men. 

```{r}
nhanes_df |> 
  pivot_longer(
    starts_with("min"),
    names_to = "minute",
    names_prefix = "min",
    values_to = "mims"
  ) |> 
  mutate(minute = as.numeric(minute)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = minute, y = mims, color = sex)) + 
  geom_line(aes(group = seqn), alpha = 0.1) + 
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) + 
  facet_grid(. ~ education) + 
  labs(
    title = "24-hour activity time course by sex and education level",
    x = "Minute of the day (1 = midnight)",
    y = "MIMS value",
    color = "Sex"
  )
```
Activity is lowest overnight (between minutes 0 to 500) for all three groups. For all three groups activity rises until midday then decreases into the evening. Men and women appear to follow the same trends.
## Problem 3
```{r}
citi_df = 
  tibble(file = list.files("data/citibike", pattern = "zip$", full.names = TRUE)) |> 
  mutate(data = map(file, read_csv, show_col_types = FALSE)) |> 
  unnest(data) |> 
  mutate(
    year = as.numeric(str_extract(file, "20[0-9]{2}")),
    month = if_else(str_detect(file, "Jan"), "January", "July"),
    month = factor(month, levels = c("January", "July")),
    weekdays = factor(
      weekdays, 
      levels = c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday")
    ),
    member_casual = factor(member_casual),
    rideable_type = factor(rideable_type)
  ) |> 
  select(-file)

dim(citi_df)

citi_df |> count(year, month)
```
```{r}
citi_df |> 
  count(year, month, member_casual) |> 
  pivot_wider(names_from = member_casual, values_from = n) |> 
  knitr::kable(
    caption = "Total Citi Bike rides by year, month and rider type",
    col.names = c("Year", "Month", "Casual", "Member")
  )
```
July has many more rides than January for both years and rider types. Members take more rides than casual riders across years and months. Casual riders make up a bigger share in July. 

```{r}
citi_df |> 
  filter(year == 2024, month == "July") |> 
  count(start_station_name, sort = TRUE) |> 
  slice_head(n = 5) |> 
  knitr::kable(
    caption = "Top 5 starting stations, July 2024",
    col.names = c("Start station", "Number of rides")
  )
```
The top 5 stations have a similar number or rides, with the highest being Pier 61 with 163 rides.

```{r}
citi_df |> 
  group_by(year, month, weekdays) |> 
  summarize(median_duration = median(duration), .groups = "drop") |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = weekdays, y = median_duration, color = month, group = month)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_line() + 
  facet_grid(. ~ year) + 
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) + 
  labs(
    title = "Median ride duration by weekday, month and year",
    x = "Day of the week",
    y = "Median ride duration (minutes)",
    color = "Month"
  )
```
July has longer median ride duration than January in both years. There was overall longer rides in 2020, possibly due to the pandemic. Weekend rides were longer across groups except for Sundays in January 2024.

```{r}
citi_df |> 
  filter(year == 2024) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = member_casual, y = duration, fill = rideable_type)) + 
  geom_boxplot() + 
  facet_grid(. ~ month) + 
  scale_y_log10() + 
  labs(
    title = "Ride duration by membership status and bike type, 2024",
    x = "Membership status",
    y = "Ride duration (minutes, log scale)",
    fill = "Bike type"
  )
```
Casual riders took longer rides than members in both months. Casual riders bike longer on classic bikes vs. the e-bikes. With members its much closer. Rides are longer in July than January. These data had many outliers so I used the log sclae.
